<div class="proj-detail-body">
  <div class="proj-detail-prose-wrap">

    <h2 class="proj-detail-h2">About the project</h2>
    <p class="proj-detail-p">Deep beneath the Atlantic Ocean, along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Lost City Hydrothermal Field rises more than 60 meters from the seafloor &mdash; a towering system of carbonate chimneys formed through serpentinization, a chemical reaction between Earth's mantle and seawater that produces hydrogen. That hydrogen fuels microbial communities and may have powered the chemical precursors to DNA billions of years ago. Astrobiologists believe similar vent systems may exist on Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus, both of which harbor liquid oceans beneath their icy crusts.</p>
    <p class="proj-detail-p">Sarah Treadwell, a graduate student in communications at the University of North Dakota, was uniquely positioned to tell this story: in April 2023, she sailed aboard the JOIDES Resolution as an outreach officer during Expedition 399 to the Lost City, the first dedicated scientific expedition to the site. During that voyage, the crew collected a record-breaking 1,267 meters of mantle rock. Treadwell's 2023 SCoPE Seed Grant project, supported through Arizona State University, transformed that first-hand experience into a planetarium show for public audiences.</p>
    <p class="proj-detail-p">The completed show premiered at the American Museum of Natural History and was also presented in Rockford, Illinois, connecting Earth's ocean floor to the broader question of life's origins in our solar system.</p>

    <div class="proj-facts-row">
      <span class="proj-fact">NASA Astrobiology Division</span>

    <h2 class="proj-detail-h2">How OpenSpace was used</h2>
    <p class="proj-detail-p">OpenSpace was used to visualize the submarine environment of the Lost City hydrothermal vent system alongside the research vessels operating there, including the JOIDES Resolution. This extended OpenSpace's visualization capabilities into underwater and astrobiology contexts, going beyond previous seafloor topography work to render a scientifically specific environment tied to a real, ongoing scientific expedition.</p>
    <p class="proj-detail-p">The resulting visuals anchored a live planetarium show that drew a direct line from Earth's ocean floor to the icy ocean moons of the outer solar system &mdash; giving audiences a visceral sense of how connected planetary science and Earth science actually are.</p>

    <div class="proj-quote">
      <p class="proj-quote-text">"Historically, the sciences have stayed largely separated. I hope this project will showcase the importance of collaboration within the sciences for astrobiology and spark interest in answering: how did we get here and are we alone?"</p>
      <p class="proj-quote-attribution">Sarah Treadwell &middot; University of North Dakota</p>
    </div>

    <div class="proj-quote">
      <p class="proj-quote-text">"This project allows us to partner with a subject matter expert to bring data into environments we haven't visualized beyond seafloor topography."</p>
      <p class="proj-quote-attribution">Rosamond Kinzler, PhD &middot; OpenSpace PI, AMNH</p>
    </div>

  </div>
</div>
